title: Заказ для вегетарианца  (An Order for the Vegetarian)

segments.t: Waitress Nastya comes into the kitchen asking Lyova to prepare a special meatless dish for the vegetarian guest in the dining room. When Lyova flatly refuses to waste time on it, Nastya sweetly convinces Max to cook vegetarian rolls for her table.
А, ну, отнеси ему, пусть ест.
Потому что я такой ерундой заниматься не буду.
Или, может, ты можешь котлеты сделать из огурцов?
Now let's break down each line of their conversation.
'A vegetarian came to our restaurant.' Mentioning a vegetarian on the spot, the "-sya" ending on "vegetarianets" ("vegetarian") marks an action that unfolds mutually or turns back on the speaker.
'And he is asking for it.' Vika answers quietly around Max, making her position completely clear.
'Made with beef pate.' Max reacts quietly in the exchange and centers the thought on "govyazhyego" ("beef", from "govyazhiy") without wasting a word.
'Only without the beef pate.' Pushing back evenly during the talk, spoken Russian compresses the whole thought into just 4 words, skipping the extra helper words English needs.
А, ну, отнеси ему, пусть ест.
'Oh, well, take it out to him and let him eat.' Max fires back lightly during the talk, bringing things back to earth after the buildup.
Потому что я такой ерундой заниматься не буду.
'Because I am not going to bother with such nonsense.' Talking about the nonsense with Max, Vika chooses "yerundoy" ("nonsense", from the root "yerunda") so Max hears the exact meaning.
Или, может, ты можешь котлеты сделать из огурцов?
'Or maybe you can make cutlets out of cucumbers?' Reacting evenly around Vika, Max keeps normal statement word order here, turning the line into a question for Vika purely through rising pitch.
'Maksim, will you make the rolls?' Vika tests wryly while looking straight at Max here.
'Oh, please.' Max warmly delivers this courtesy word in the exchange using "pozhaluysta" ("please") — the all-purpose Russian politeness word that covers both "please" and "you're welcome".
'You really know how to persuade someone.' Pushing back plainly in the exchange, spoken Russian compresses the whole thought into just 2 words, skipping the extra helper words English needs.

'Thank you, Maksish.' Max lightly voices this word of thanks at this moment using "spasibo" ("thank you") — the everyday word for "thank you", which grew out of the old blessing "spasi Bog" ("God save you").

'Go on. Thank you.' Vika smoothly delivers this word of thanks toward Max using "spasibo" ("thank you") — the everyday word for "thank you", which grew out of the old blessing "spasi Bog" ("God save you").
'Alright, I was joking.' Max evenly uses this word of agreement in front of Vika using "ladno" ("alright") — built from the old Russian root for harmony and order, used every day for "okay, fine".
А, ну, отнеси ему, пусть ест.
Потому что я такой ерундой заниматься не буду.
Или, может, ты можешь котлеты сделать из огурцов?
That wraps up this scene as nastya asks Lyova to prepare a meatless dish for her vegetarian guest, and when Lyova refuses, she persuades Max to make vegetable rolls instead. See you next time!
